videoTitle: North Korea Robbed Binance Via A DevOps Laptop
videoDescription:
0:00 The Claude Code update that wasn't Anthropic's  
3:19 The checkout that took one cent  
4:49 Six billion dollars in twenty minutes

About $6.3 billion left Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, in roughly 20 minutes on October 29, the largest crypto theft on record. Binance points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop plus additional points of breach. TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute it to North Korea's TraderTraitor, the group behind the 2025 Bybit theft. About $2.7 billion in stablecoins was frozen; Binance says it will cover the losses. Kevin Beaumont says Binance uses Claude Code on Cursor, and the theft started inside the window when a backdoored Claude Code extension was live there; none of the companies has tied the two together.

Claude Code in Cursor: for about eleven hours on October 29, Cursor's extension marketplace served tampered versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension (2.1.312 and 2.1.313) through Anthropic's official account there. A 66-line loader added an attacker's SSH key, tried to open a reverse SSH tunnel, set up persistence, and sent host details home. Bugs in the malware stopped the tunnel on most Mac and Windows machines, but the key and persistence stay even after you update. If you used Claude Code in Cursor that day, run Cursor's check for the svc-telemetry key and follow its remediation steps. Anthropic says its own systems weren't compromised; Cursor hasn't said how the upload happened.

Drupal: Commerce Core has an actively exploited access-bypass flaw (CVE-2026-118539) used to tamper with orders, including one-cent prices. Update to Commerce Core 3.3.13 or 8.x-2.41 and audit recent orders.

videoTitle: Who actually runs a Kubernetes cluster? ⚓ #kubernetes #k8s #devops #cloudnative
videoDescription:
Who actually runs a cluster? There's no one at the wheel. Just a few programs, each with one small job. ⚓

🏢 The control plane is the harbour office.
🛎️ The API server is the front desk. Everything goes through it.
📖 etcd is the log book, where the cluster's state is kept.
🗺️ The scheduler picks a node for each new pod, but starts nothing.
👀 The controllers watch, and fix what drifts.
👨‍✈️ Every node has its own captain, the kubelet. It makes sure the pods on its node are running.
🔀 kube-proxy keeps the network rules for Services.

So you apply a file, the API server stores it in etcd, a controller creates the pods, the scheduler picks a node for each, and the kubelet on that node starts them.

Part 2 of Kubernetes in a minute.

videoTitle: What a Helm .prov file does before you install a chart
videoDescription:
Should you install a Helm chart you were handed?

You hold the .tgz, its .prov file and the publisher's public key.
Import the key into your GPG keyring, then run helm verify with the .prov next to the archive.
If verification fails, the install aborts before the chart renders.
Skip the check and the install trusts the registry login alone.

Follow for more practical ops checks.

Video includes AI-generated imagery. Recreations are illustrative.
Sources:
- Helm Chart Signing and Provenance with Cosign · DevCloudLab: https://devcloudlab.com/blog/helm-chart-signing-provenance-cosign
- Package, Sign, and Verify Charts: https://kodekloud.com/blog/package-sign-and-verify-charts

videoTitle: What Is Progressive Delivery? Canary, Blue-Green and Feature Flags
videoDescription:
🚀 The Automation Stack — Bite-sized tech for developers who want to stay ahead.

What is progressive delivery? The umbrella over canary releases, blue-green deployments and feature flags, gradual rollouts that ship a change to a few users first, tested in a small model.

THE IDEA

Ship a new version to everyone, and if it is broken, everyone finds out. Progressive delivery ships to a few people first, lets a number judge it, and only then goes wider. Argo Rollouts defines it as releasing updates in a controlled and gradual manner, reducing the risk of the release.

THE MODEL

I built a small Python model to compare the tools. 1000 requests, and a new version that fails 1 request in 10.

      def handle(self, request):
          self.served += 1
          return self.served % 10 != 0

THE FIRST SURPRISE

Deploying code and releasing it to users are two different moves. Blue-green splits them with two identical environments. Blue serves everyone, green gets the new version with nobody on it. Test green, switch the router, and if anything breaks, switch it back. But the switch is all or nothing. In the model green passed a 5 request test, went live, and 100 of 1000 requests failed.

  green deployed, live requests on it: 0
  private test on green: 5 requests, 5 passed
  router to green: 1000 of 1000 requests
  failed: 100
  router back to blue: one change

THE CANARY

A canary sends a slice of real traffic to the new version and keeps the rest on the old one. The name comes from coal miners, whose caged canary met the gas before they did.

A NUMBER DECIDES, NOT A PERSON

In Argo Rollouts' own example, step one puts 20 percent of traffic on the canary, and a check reads its success rate. The example rule wants at least 0.95. The model's canary managed 0.90, so the check failed, the rollout aborted itself and the canary weight went back to zero. 20 requests failed, not 100.

        steps:
        - setWeight: 20
        - pause: {duration: 10m}
        - setWeight: 40
        - pause: {duration: 10m}

FEATURE FLAGS

A feature flag puts the switch inside the code. The new path ships turned off, so deploying it releases nothing. Turn it on for 10 percent of users, picked by user number, and each person always gets the same answer. In the model 10 requests failed, and turning the flag off put everyone back on the old path with no new deploy.

  def checkout(user_id, old, new):
      if flag_on("new-checkout", user_id):
          return new(user_id)
      return old(user_id)

  flag at 0%: 0 users on the new path
  flag at 10%: 100 of 1000 users on it
  failed: 10
  same users on a second pass: True
  flag at 0% again: 0 users, no deploy

WHERE YOUR SWITCH LIVES

Blue-green keeps it in the router and gives you the fastest way back. A canary keeps it in the traffic and lets a number stop a bad version. A flag keeps it in the code and picks exactly who sees it.

Never bet every user on one deploy. Show it to a few, let the numbers vote, then go wide.

videoTitle: Health Check That Took Down Our API
videoDescription:
Kubernetes liveness probes explained through a cascading API outage. Three replicas share a slow database, and a database-dependent health endpoint turns that slowdown into repeated container restarts.

We follow client traffic, inspect the failed probe, and trace a kubelet health check into the shared database. Then we replay the same slowdown with an implemented local liveness check. The database still needs to recover, while the corrected check avoids unnecessary container restarts.

Readiness is a separate app-specific decision. Checking the same shared dependency there can also remove every replica from traffic.

This is a simplified teaching scenario. Pod identities remain stable during container restarts; the corrected sequence is explicitly an alternate replay.

videoTitle: The docs showed it. Your proxy refused it.
videoDescription:
You find exactly the limit you need in your proxy's docs: a request limit per customer. You paste it into your config. Your proxy won't start: unknown field.

The docs describe the newest release. Your production runs the exact version you pinned, and that field arrived after it. The binary you run has never heard of it.

The fix:
1. Put every config through the validator of the binary you actually ship (the same image tag as production), before anything depends on it. It answers OK, or why not.
2. Ship what it accepts: one shared rate limit, a ceiling for every caller. At three requests a minute, the fourth is refused with 429 Too Many Requests.
3. Write down what waits for an upgrade, and who decides it.

Validate against what runs. The docs are a promise about a different version.

Not covered here: a shared limit is a backstop against runaway spend, not fairness (one busy caller can use up everyone's share until the per-customer limit arrives); how clients should back off on a 429 (the Retry-After header); and reading the docs for your own version, which helps but does not replace the validator.

Narrated with a synthetic voice.

videoTitle: Fix JWT Clock Skew in 2 Steps ⭐ (Part 6/9) #backend #jwt #programming
videoDescription:
Fixing JWT clock skew takes two steps. Step 1: NTP. Your server asks a time server "what time is it?", adds the travel time, and slowly corrects its clock, checking again every few minutes.

Step 2: NTP makes clocks close, not equal, so add a small grace period: clockTolerance: 30 in jwt.verify (other libraries call it leeway). 30 seconds fixes false errors; an hour would just help attackers. Part 6 of 9.

▶️ Full video: 4 Ways JWT Breaks in Production (and the Fixes)

videoTitle: How does Kubernetes decide where a pod fits? ⚓ #kubernetes #k8s #devops #shorts
videoDescription:
Every ship has limited deck space. So how does Kubernetes decide where a pod fits? ⚓

📦 You tell it. A request is what the pod needs: the scheduler finds a node with room, and that space is reserved.
📏 A limit is the ceiling. Go over the CPU limit and it's slowed down. Go over memory and it can be OOMKilled.
🧮 CPU is counted in cores, so 500m is half a core.
📈 The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler checks about every 15 seconds and adds or removes pods to meet your target.
🔧 It needs a metrics server, and requests to be set.

Part 12 of Kubernetes in a minute.

videoTitle: Your container is running. It might still be broken ⚓ #kubernetes #k8s #shorts
videoDescription:
A container can be running and still be stuck. Kubernetes can't tell, unless you teach it how. ⚓

💓 A liveness probe asks: are you still alive? If it keeps failing, the kubelet restarts the container.
🚦 A readiness probe asks: ready for visitors? If it fails, the pod leaves the Service, but isn't restarted.
🐢 A startup probe is for slow starters: the other checks wait until it passes.
🔌 A probe can call a web path, open a TCP port, or run a command.
⚠️ Keep liveness simple. If it checks your database, a database hiccup can restart every pod.

videoTitle: Docker Image Layers Explained | Cloud & Infrastructure Explained #02
videoDescription:
Change one line of code and your whole Docker build starts over? Move one line in the Dockerfile and most of it comes straight from cache. This short opens up a Docker image: a stack of read-only layers, a thin writable container layer with copy-on-write, content-addressed layers shared between images, and how the build cache really works.

Key takeaways:
- An image is a stack of read-only layers; each one stores only what changed (files added, modified or deleted)
- RUN, COPY and ADD create filesystem layers; ENV and CMD only change the image config
- A running container adds one thin writable layer on top; changed files are copied up first (copy-on-write), and an overlay filesystem like overlay2 merges everything into one view
- Layers are identified by a content digest, so images built on the same base share those layers on disk
- Build cache: a changed step rebuilds that layer and every layer after it, so put rarely-changing steps first (COPY requirements.txt, RUN pip install, then COPY . .)
- Deleting files in a later layer doesn't shrink the image: clean up in the same RUN
- Secrets copied in and deleted later stay in the layers: use build secrets (RUN --mount=type=secret)
- Use a .dockerignore, multi-stage builds for small images, and docker history to inspect layers

Full courses on Infinity Systems: https://www.youtube.com/@infinitysys-org

Sources:
- Docker build cache: https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/
- Build cache invalidation: https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/invalidation/
- Multi-stage builds: https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/
- Storage drivers (layers, copy-on-write): https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/
- OverlayFS storage driver (overlay2): https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/overlayfs-driver/
- Build secrets: https://docs.docker.com/build/building/secrets/
- Build context and .dockerignore: https://docs.docker.com/build/concepts/context/

videoTitle: base64 isn't encryption: ConfigMaps and Secrets ⚓ #kubernetes #k8s #devops #shorts
videoDescription:
One image, running in dev and in production. But the settings differ, so don't bake them in. ⚓

🗒️ A ConfigMap holds plain settings as keys and values. Pods get them as environment variables or files.
🔑 A Secret holds passwords and tokens, used the same way.
👀 But the values are only base64. That's encoding, not encryption: anyone who can read the Secret can read the value.
🔒 By default, Secrets sit unencrypted in etcd. Turn on encryption at rest, and give out access sparingly.
♻️ Environment variables are read when the container starts, so changing them means restarting the pod.

Part 8 of Kubernetes in a minute.

videoTitle: MCP Explained for DevOps Engineers in 10 Minutes
videoDescription:
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol in which an AI host's client calls tools on an MCP server. The model only proposes the call; it never executes it.
In 10 minutes, MCP explained for DevOps engineers, built as one diagram you can redraw from memory.

Subscribe for a new cloud and DevOps explainer every week: https://www.youtube.com/@InfraNarrative?sub_confirmation=1

What you'll learn:
- Host → client → server: each client holds exactly one connection to one server, and who actually runs your tool call
- The message sequence: initialize / tools/list / tools/call up to the November 2025 revision, and the stateless core in the July 28, 2026 revision
- stdio vs Streamable HTTP, when each is used, and how remote servers authenticate with OAuth 2.1
- A three-item safety checklist: scoped credentials, read-only by default, approval for write actions. Plus how to watch real messages in MCP Inspector

Spec revisions, flags and versions change. Everything here is as stated in the video. Check the current docs before relying on it.

videoTitle: What is Docker? Images and containers in under a minute
videoDescription:
Docker packs your app, its runtime and its dependencies into an image that never changes once built. Running an image gives you a container, an isolated process, and one image can start many. Unlike a virtual machine, a container doesn't boot its own operating system; containers share the host's kernel, so they start fast, and the same image runs on your laptop, in testing and in production.

Transcript:
Job ads say DevOps engineer, or SRE. What do these people do all day? At the end: the part job ads rarely mention.
For this lesson you need nothing. Just watch.
No terminal and no code. Only pictures.
About five minutes.

== The plan ==
This is lesson seven of DevOps from Zero.
First, two job titles, explained.
Then an example day.
Then what happens when things break.
And the skills the job really needs.

== Two titles ==
  - DevOps engineer — Builds the road from code to users, and keeps it working (like the person who designs and runs the kitchen line)
First title: DevOps engineer. This person builds the road from code to users, and keeps it working. Like the person who runs the kitchen line.
  - SRE — Site reliability engineer: keeps a service reliable, using software (like the manager who makes every dinner service run smoothly)
Second title: SRE, short for site reliability engineer. This person keeps a service reliable, and uses software to do it.
The two titles share a lot: production, automation, and being on call. The DevOps engineer leans toward the road. The SRE leans toward reliability.

== A day ==
Here is an example day. Every team is different. In the morning, look at the dashboards, and at any night alerts.
Then, improve the pipeline, to make it faster or safer.
Review a colleague's change, before it is merged.
In the afternoon, automate a boring job.
And write down what you learned.

== Incidents ==
  - incident — Something is broken for users, right now (like the oven dies in the middle of dinner service)
Some days are not calm. An incident means something is broken for users, right now. Like an oven dying during dinner service.
During an incident, the order matters. First, stop the harm, for example with a rollback. Then find the cause, and fix it for good.
  - postmortem — A written review after an incident: what happened, how to prevent it (like the team talk after a bad night: no blame, better habits)
After the incident comes the postmortem. It is a written review: what happened, and how to prevent it. With no blame.

== So far ==
So far: the DevOps engineer cares for the road, and the SRE for reliability.
On calm days, they improve, review, and automate.
During incidents, they stop the harm, find the cause, and write it down.
Next: the skills, and the part job ads rarely mention.

== Skills ==
What skills does the job need? Linux and the terminal, first.
Automation: scripts, and tools like Ansible.
Containers and Kubernetes.
Networks, version control, logs and metrics.
Nobody knows everything. You learn one piece at a time.

== The hidden part ==
Now, the part job ads rarely mention: writing. Clear notes that others can follow.
Asking: a good question saves hours.
And explaining, to colleagues who are not engineers.
  - runbook — Written steps for a known problem, so anyone can fix it (like the card on the kitchen wall: what to do if the oven fails)
One example of that writing: a runbook. It holds written steps for a known problem, so anyone can fix it. Even at night.

videoTitle: Transformasi Model ke Teks (M2T) dengan Epsilon EGL & EGX | Advanced Software Engineering & DevOps
videoDescription:
Bagaimana menghasilkan kode, data, atau dokumentasi langsung dari model? Pelajari transformasi model ke teks (M2T) dengan Epsilon EGL, EGX, dan EOL.

Sesi ini melanjutkan studi kasus MediaFlow dalam mata kuliah Advanced Software Engineering dan DevOps. Model pipeline video yang tersimpan dalam XMI diubah menjadi dua artefak web untuk Mediaflow Viewer: JSON untuk Eclipse Layout Kernel (ELK), yang menghitung tata letak graf, dan fragmen HTML berisi statistik serta tabel node dan edge untuk panel samping. Pekerjaannya dibagi ke tiga bahasa Epsilon: EGX mengatur multi-output, EGL menyusun teks, dan EOL menyimpan helper yang dipakai kedua template. Transformasinya dijalankan dari runner Java di luar Eclipse, lalu hasilnya dimuat oleh viewer di browser.

Di dunia teks tidak ada metamodel yang menjaga keabsahan hasil. Satu koma yang tertinggal atau satu tanda petik yang tidak di-escape sudah cukup membuat seluruh berkas ditolak konsumennya, sehingga output harus benar secara semantik sekaligus valid secara leksikal. Karena itu sesi ini juga membahas id yang stabil, escaping, referensi port ke node, dan validasi output yang bisa diotomasi layaknya regression test.

Yang dibahas dalam video ini:
- Perbedaan transformasi model ke teks dan model ke model, serta posisinya dalam Model-Driven Engineering
- Studi kasus Mediaflow Viewer: mengapa XMI perlu diturunkan menjadi format web
- Tabel pemetaan Graph, Node, Port, dan Edge ke JSON ELK dan fragmen HTML
- Arsitektur proyek M2T dan struktur foldernya
- Aturan EGX yang membangkitkan dua berkas dari setiap Graph
- Helper EOL: jsonValue, jsonEscape, isOut, sourceNode, dan targetNode
- Template EGL untuk JSON ELK: id node dan port yang stabil serta opsi layout ELK
- Template EGL untuk fragmen HTML berisi statistik, tabel node, dan tabel edge
- Runner Java dengan EmfModel, EglFileGeneratingTemplateFactory, dan EgxModule
- Viewer JavaScript yang memuat JSON dan HTML lewat fetch dan cache
- Evaluasi output pada dua model input: kelengkapan, konsistensi struktur, kebenaran referensi, dan validitas format
- Lima jebakan umum, dari JSON yang rusak karena escaping hingga cross-site scripting dan protokol file

Di akhir sesi ada latihan mengubah arah layout dari RIGHT menjadi DOWN untuk menguji apakah aturan sisi port EAST dan WEST masih cocok. Sesi berikutnya membahas validasi model.

Daftar isi:
0:00 Pembukaan dan tujuan pembelajaran
3:07 Transformasi model ke teks vs model ke model

Monitoring menjawab apa yang salah, observabilitas menjawab mengapa. Pelajari cara membuat sistem terdistribusi dapat diamati dengan Prometheus dan Grafana.

Setiap node memancarkan metrik runtime lewat endpoint /metrics miliknya sendiri, Prometheus menjemput metrik tersebut setiap dua detik dengan model pull-based, lalu Grafana menyajikannya dalam dashboard. Dari angka-angka itu kita membaca profil beban setiap komponen, menguji dampak bertambahnya penonton, dan menunjuk node yang bermasalah tanpa membuka satu baris kode pun.

- Counter, Gauge, dan Histogram dalam satu pustaka metrik bersama, beserta label service, instance, dan topic atau stage
- Server metrik di setiap node dengan port berbeda dan validasi port saat startup
- Pola stopwatch untuk latensi tiap tahap serta latensi end-to-end dari cap waktu di header pesan

- Prometheus dan Grafana di docker-compose.yml, scrape interval di prometheus.yml, dan alasan memakai nama service Docker, bukan localhost
- Menghubungkan Grafana ke Prometheus sebagai data source
- Skenario kegagalan: transformer dihentikan, video membeku, dan metrik menunjukkan penyebabnya
- Hasil eksperimen: capturer dan transformer berat di CPU, broker ringan, web server berat di memori
- Eksperimen satu versus enam klien MJPEG: latensi tetap sekitar 30 milidetik, memori naik sekitar 5 MB per klien

videoTitle: Can AI Troubleshoot Kubernetes Problems Let's Test
videoDescription:
Can AI troubleshoot Kubernetes CrashLoopBackOff errors? In this hands-on DevOps lab, I test **kagent**, an open-source Kubernetes-native AI agent platform, to investigate a real Kubernetes Pod failure using **OpenAI GPT-4.1-mini and MCP tools**.

Instead of manually digging through Kubernetes events, container logs, and configurations, I let an AI agent investigate a failing application called `demo-webapp`.

Watch how kagent inspects the Pod, analyzes Kubernetes events and logs, identifies a missing `DATABASE_URL` environment variable, and recommends the fix.

Can AI really find the root cause? Let's find out!

In this tutorial, you'll learn how AI-assisted Kubernetes troubleshooting works, how to debug CrashLoopBackOff errors, and why human approval and verification still matter in DevOps operations.

⏱️ VIDEO CHAPTERS

01:00 – What Is kagent? AI Agents for Kubernetes  
01:59 – Meet the k8s-troubleshooter AI Agent  
02:48 – Checking the Failing Kubernetes Deployment

04:36 – Starting the AI Troubleshooting Investigation  
05:40 – MCP Tool Calls: Pods, Events and Logs  
06:05 – Human Approval for Kubernetes Tool Access  
07:00 – AI Finds the Root Cause: Missing DATABASE_URL  
08:28 – Applying the Recommended Fix  
09:22 – Verifying the Kubernetes Rollout  
10:21 – Pod Running: Checking Container Logs  
11:11 – Can AI Replace Kubernetes Engineers?  
12:15 – Final Thoughts and Next Tutorials  

💻 KUBERNETES COMMANDS – COPY & PASTE

Check Deployment and Pod status:

kubectl get deployments -n ai-demo
kubectl get pods -n ai-demo


Inspect Kubernetes events and container logs manually:

kubectl describe pod  POD_NAME  -n ai-demo
kubectl logs POD_NAME  -n ai-demo --previous


Apply the fix demonstrated in this lab:

kubectl -n ai-demo set env deployment/demo-webapp DATABASE_URL='postgresql://demo-db:5432/appdb'


Verify the application recovery:

kubectl -n ai-demo rollout status deployment/demo-webapp --timeout=120s
kubectl get deployments -n ai-demo
kubectl get pods -n ai-demo
kubectl logs -n ai-demo deployment/demo-webapp

Lab note: 'DATABASE_URL' is a sample value. This demo application checks whether the environment variable exists; it does not connect to a real PostgreSQL database.

videoTitle: Docker container asal mein kya hai? #Shorts
videoDescription:
Series: Docker & DevOps: 0 se Hero · Episode 3 · Playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLLjZSteUjQTQ

"Mere laptop pe toh chal raha tha!" Is problem ka jawab hai container. Par container koi chhota computer nahi hai. Woh server par chalta ek aam process hai, jise kernel ek alag duniya dikhata hai. Is video mein real Docker run par dekhiye.

Key takeaways:
• App ko sirf code nahi, poora environment chahiye. Hamari app laptop par chali (Python 3.15 + tabulate), server par error aaya (Python 3.12, tabulate nahi).
• Image = app + uska environment, files ki layers mein, saath mein start command. Real sizes: Debian 110 MB, Python 48.3 MB, tabulate 11.6 MB, hamari app 12.3 kB.
• Container = image se chala ek process, jise kernel namespaces se apni files, hostname, network aur process numbers dikhata hai.
• Proof: wahi process container ke andar PID 1 hai aur server par PID 2140 (NSpid: 2140 1).
• Gotcha: container apna kernel nahi laata. Andar Debian, bahar Ubuntu, kernel dono jagah Linux 6.8.
• Mera poora demo Mac par chal rahi ek Linux virtual machine ke andar tha. Agla episode (DevOps · 4): VM kya hai, aur container usse halka kyun hai?

Sources:
• Real run: Docker 29.1.3, Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 6.8.0-147, 17 Nov 2026; re-run 21 Nov 2026. PIDs har run mein alag hote hain.
• Docker docs, What is a container?: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-a-container/
• Docker docs, What is an image?: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-an-image/
• Docker docs, Storage drivers: https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/
• namespaces(7): https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/namespaces.7.html
• pid_namespaces(7): https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/pid_namespaces.7.html
• mount_namespaces(7): https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/mount_namespaces.7.html
• proc_pid_status(5): https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc_pid_status.5.html
• OCI runtime spec: https://github.com/opencontainers/runtime-spec

Related: Docker & DevOps · 2 (Program vs process)
Music & sound effects: original, made for Server Side Story.

videoTitle: Docker Port Published to Everyone? Bind Localhost
videoDescription:
Docker publishes a port on all host interfaces by default. For local-only access, bind the host port to loopback:

docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx

Port mapping format: HOST_IP:HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT

Docker docs:
https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/running-containers/publishing-ports/
